about: Machine-readable provenance for the written findings in docs/findings/*.md. Each claim lists the metric values that corroborate it (as <results file>:<dot.path>), the procedure, the data sources and the code that produced it. tests/test_findings_registry.py checks every listed value against the results files, so prose and numbers cannot drift apart silently.

conventions.metric_ref: <file under results/>:<dot.separated.path>; keyed dicts (e.g. by_combination.<model>|<condition>) rather than list indices; keys containing dots (e.g. code labels like F5.1) cannot be addressed — expose a plain scalar key instead
conventions.unit: Majority label per fragment x model x prompt condition unless stated; corrected (accuracy-only) scoring; locked gold 2026-10-03 unless stated
conventions.status: agreed = wording agreed with the author; draft = discussed, wording open
conventions.headlines: Finding headlines lead with a local implication, followed by the observation that warrants it (2026-11-13); previous_headline keeps the descriptive version.

findings.research_question: To what extent can large language models accurately assess the quality of evaluative reasoning?
findings.headline: Models are not yet reliable judges of evaluative reasoning: they agreed with the expert 60% of the time, modestly above chance, and caught flawed reasoning far less reliably than they affirmed sound reasoning.

claims.text: LLMs agreed with the expert on ~60% of fragments (95% CI 54-66%).
claims.procedure: Pooled fragment-level pass rate across 6 models x 2 conditions x 150 fragments; 95% CI by fragment-clustered bootstrap (5,000 resamples, seed 42).

claims.text: Modestly above chance: kappa ~0.20.
claims.procedure: Cohen's kappa, model majority label vs locked gold, per model x condition (12), averaged.

claims.text: Below the expert's own test-retest consistency (85%, kappa = 0.70).
claims.procedure: RC1: anchor re-classified 20 random fragments blind; percent agreement and Cohen's kappa.

claims.text: Models affirmed sound reasoning far more reliably than they detected flawed reasoning (75% vs 44%).
claims.procedure: Accuracy within each gold label, per model x condition, averaged.

claims.text: No significant differences between the six models or between closed and open models.
claims.procedure: Chi-squared test of pass/fail across six models (df = 5); two-proportion z-test closed vs open.

claims.text: Run-to-run consistency: all three runs agreed in 86.8% of combinations.
claims.procedure: Share of fragment x model x condition combinations with 3/3 runs passing or 3/3 failing.

methods_notes.text: Deviation: pre-registered scoring with the coherence gate gave 43.3%; RC3 found 0 of 217 sampled flagged runs incoherent, so the gate was removed.
methods_notes.procedure: As-designed pass rate from the pre-registered outcomes. RC3: stratified human review of coherence-flagged runs; rule-of-three (3/n) upper bound on the incoherence rate per stratum, applied to the unreviewed remainder.
methods_notes.caveat: The rater never assigned 'incoherent' (including 94 controls), so RC3 cannot fully separate a mis-firing pipeline from a high personal threshold for incoherence.

findings.previous_headline: Models agreed with the expert 60% of the time, modestly above chance and well below the expert's own consistency, and they caught flawed reasoning far less reliably than they affirmed sound reasoning.

findings.research_question: To what extent can large language models accurately assess the quality of evaluative reasoning?
findings.headline: Expert judgment is a contested yardstick: models agreed with the expert about as often as two trained evaluators did (about 57% vs 55–61%).

claims.text: Comparable to trained human evaluators' agreement with the same expert's independent ratings.
claims.procedure: Percent agreement on the 38 RC2 fragments in the benchmark: each human rater vs the anchor's pass-2 (independent) ratings; each model x condition majority label vs the same, averaged.
claims.caveat: Small (n = 38) and not held out; against the locked gold, humans agree at 68-74% but that comparison is partly circular (gold revised toward the raters).

claims.text: Rises to ~74% when contested labels are resolved by an independent third reviewer; the adjustment can only raise the figure.
claims.procedure: Label-substitution sensitivity: the third reviewer's blind call replaces the gold on the 35 fragments where >= 5 of 6 models agreed against it; rescored and re-adjudicated.

claims.text: Roughly one in four fragments split qualified evaluators.
claims.procedure: Two independent estimates: disagreement between the two RC2 raters (40 fragments) and the share of benchmark fragments in the contested set (35/150).

claims.text: 10 of the 35 contested fragments were pre-lock revisions; on all 10 the anchor's original rating matched the models and the third reviewer sided with the models. The 4 also rated by the RC2 raters are each a 2-2 human split.
claims.procedure: Join of the contested review with the pre-lock revision supplement and the RC2 blind-retest ratings; human votes = two RC2 raters, the anchor's original rating, and the third reviewer.

findings.previous_headline: Matching the expert was hard for everyone: models agreed with the expert about as often as two trained evaluators did (about 57% vs 55–61%).

findings.research_question: To what extent can large language models accurately assess the quality of evaluative reasoning?
findings.headline: The benchmark likely understates model capability: on re-review, most of the primary model's apparent failures rested on labels the expert no longer defended.

claims.text: Of 76 failed passages, 28 were confirmed and 48 rested on labels the expert no longer defended; failure rate 37.3% to 14.0%.
claims.procedure: Expert re-review of every GPT failure with GPT's rationale in view: coded as genuine failure (Appendix D.1) or coder_doubts_gold_standard.
claims.caveat: Not independent; one-sided (failures only), so 14% is biased downward; RC4 pending.

claims.text: The expert sided with the model on 32 of 33 stricter calls but 16 of 43 more lenient ones.
claims.procedure: Disposition split by error direction (fragment level).

claims.text: An independent third reviewer sided with the models on 25 of 35 contested passages.
claims.procedure: Blind classification of the 35 contested fragments by a third reviewer.

claims.text: The expert's own re-review of the primary model's errors confirmed most lenient errors (27 of 43) and attributed nearly all strict errors (32 of 33) to the gold standard.
claims.procedure: GPT failure coding: each failed fragment either coded as a genuine failure (Appendix D.1) or marked coder_doubts_gold_standard; split by error direction.
claims.caveat: Not independent: the expert reconsidering the expert's own labels with GPT's rationale in view.

findings.research_question: What systematic failure patterns emerge from the LLM artifacts?
findings.headline: Switching models is unlikely to fix these errors: the six models got the same passages wrong, so what mattered was which passage was judged, not which model judged it.

claims.text: 31 passages were failed by every model and 35 by none, versus about 2 of each expected if models erred independently.
claims.procedure: A model fails a fragment if it fails in either condition. Expected counts: exact Poisson-binomial from each model's own any-condition fail rate, assuming independence.

claims.text: Which passage was judged explained about half the variation in outcomes; which model, almost none.
claims.procedure: Eta squared (between-group share of variance) of binary fail across 1,800 combinations, by fragment, model and condition separately.

claims.text: Nearly all of the primary model's failures (107 of 112) were shared with at least two other models. Because failures are almost all shared and the codes describe flaws in the passage, the flaws in GPT's coded failures likely describe what other models missed too; why each model missed them was coded for GPT only.
claims.procedure: H.4 challenge cases. Criterion 1: GPT fails AND >= 2 comparison models fail on the same fragment x condition. Criterion 2: primary code accounting for >= 10% of confirmed coded rows.
claims.caveat: Generalizes which flaws go undetected on shared failures, not each model's reasoning; failures by other models on passages GPT got right are not covered.

claims.text: Of the 31 passages every model failed, 26 were contested; expert review confirmed 13 as genuine errors and doubted the gold on 18.
claims.procedure: Cross-tabulation of the all-six fragments with the contested set, the gold label and the GPT coding disposition.

findings.previous_headline: The six models got the same passages wrong: what mattered was which passage was being judged, not which model judged it.

findings.research_question: What systematic failure patterns emerge from the LLM artifacts?
findings.headline: Used as reviewers, models would let weak reasoning through: they missed flawed reasoning more often than they rejected sound reasoning. Without examples, the lean depended on passage length: none on short passages, about 2 to 1 on long ones. The study's calibration examples amplified it at every length, to about 5 to 1 on long passages.

claims.text: Without examples, models called flawed passages sound 50% of the time and sound passages flawed 33% of the time (1.5 to 1), consistently across the three label versions (1.4 to 1.5).
claims.procedure: Within-label error rates of zero-shot majority labels against the locked gold, the anchor's pre-revision ratings, and the triangulated labels.
claims.caveat: Length-dependent (see RQ2.2.h) and comes from three of six models (Gemini, GLM, Kimi).

claims.text: With the study's calibration examples the gap widened to 62% vs 16% (nearly 4 to 1), holding under every label version (3.6 to 4.7); pooled across conditions the ratio is about 2 to 1.
claims.procedure: As RQ2.2.a for few-shot majority labels; pooled ratio across both conditions for reference.
claims.caveat: One fixed calibration set (two examples, fixed order) was tested; the amplification is a property of that set, not of few-shot prompting in general.

claims.text: Three models were lenient in both conditions; GPT, Claude and DeepSeek leaned strict at zero-shot and turned lenient with few-shot examples.
claims.procedure: Per model x condition: lenient if missed-flaw rate exceeds wrongly-rejected rate; few-shot more lenient if share called sound rises from zero-shot.

claims.text: The expert's own re-review points the same way: 27 of 43 lenient errors confirmed vs 1 of 33 strict.
claims.procedure: GPT failure coding disposition by error direction (fragment level).
claims.caveat: Direction confirmation exists for GPT only, and the re-review is not independent of the expert's labels.

claims.text: Per-model tables in rq2.md: missed-flaw and wrongly-rejected rates, and share called sound, by model and condition.
claims.procedure: Per model x condition majority labels vs locked gold; within-label error rates and share of sound calls.

claims.text: On the 38 RC2 passages, within each condition the ratio is similar whichever human judge is the reference: zero-shot 0.78-0.85 (slightly strict), few-shot 1.98-3.05 (lenient). The judge matters little; the condition and the sample matter a lot.
claims.procedure: On RC2 fragments in the benchmark, model majority labels scored against each human judge in turn, per prompt condition; ratio of within-label error rates.
claims.caveat: n = 38; ratios on this subset differ from the full 150 for every judge, the locked gold included, so it speaks to judge-dependence, not to overall size.

claims.text: Leniency accounts for apparent criterion differences: once the share of flawed passages is held constant, criterion explains nothing (p = .94); the lenient gap appears within all seven criteria in both conditions.
claims.procedure: Fragment-level fail proportion regressed on gold label, then label + criterion; nested F test with a permutation p-value shuffling criterion within label strata; per condition. Gold composition chi-squared; models' own not-sound share by criterion (permutation).
claims.caveat: Small groups (7-35 fragments per criterion); a modest criterion effect could go undetected. Impact vs relevance gold difference (Fisher p = .029) was chosen post hoc and is not interpreted.

claims.text: Leniency grows with passage length: zero-shot ratio 0.87 (short) to 2.26 (long); few-shot 2.64 to 5.43. Models' own share of sound calls rises with length while the expert's does not.
claims.procedure: Paragraph-count bins (1-3, 4-6, 7+); leniency ratio per bin and condition with fragment-clustered bootstrap CIs; Spearman correlation of word count with models' share of sound calls per fragment.
claims.caveat: Length may proxy for other features (evidence volume, structure, evaluative language); mechanism untested (lexicon test parked for RQ3). Bins chosen after the RC2 subset (1-3 paragraphs) prompted the check.

claims.text: The leniency ratio's uncertainty: zero-shot 1.52 (CI 1.14-2.01), few-shot 3.79 (CI 2.67-5.89), pooled 2.27 (CI 1.73-3.07); the RC2 subset's zero-shot 0.78 is matched by only 0.2-0.4% of random 38-passage subsets.
claims.procedure: Fragment-clustered bootstrap (5,000, seed 42) of the pooled within-label error-rate ratio; 5,000 random 38-fragment subsets drawn freely and with the RC2 subset's label mix.

claims.text: GPT re-review by length: F5.1 accounts for about half of confirmed failures at every length; strict failures concentrate in short passages but the gold was doubted on strict failures at every length (16/17, 9/9, 7/7).
claims.procedure: GPT fragment-level coding disposition and codes cross-tabulated with paragraph-count bins.
claims.caveat: GPT only; small cells (5-17); re-review not independent of the expert's labels.

findings.previous_headline: Models were lenient judges: they missed flawed reasoning more often than they rejected sound reasoning. Without examples, the lean depended on passage length: none on short passages, about 2 to 1 on long ones. The study's calibration examples amplified it at every length, to about 5 to 1 on long passages.

findings.research_question: What systematic failure patterns emerge from the LLM artifacts?
findings.headline: Models might be taken in by evaluative veneer: their most common genuine failure was passing conclusions that discuss performance without ever saying how good it was, and the study's calibration examples made it worse.

claims.text: F5.1 (evaluative judgment absent) is the most common primary code among confirmed failures: 13 of 28, about half at every length.
claims.procedure: Primary codes among fragments the expert confirmed as genuine GPT failures (Appendix D.1); cross-tabulated with paragraph-count bins.
claims.caveat: Primary model only; one coder; RC4 pending; boundary of what counts as a judgment.

claims.text: With the calibration examples GPT missed more judgment-absent passages (13 vs 7 confirmed rows); all 13 F5.1 fragments failed with examples, 6 only with them.
claims.procedure: F5.1 among confirmed failure rows by prompt condition; conditions in which each F5.1 fragment failed.
claims.caveat: Small numbers; example content, order and length confounded.

claims.text: The extra misses introduced by the examples mostly lacked both a judgment and adequate evidence (5 of 6 carry F2.2), so the 'no judgment and no evidence' boundary account does not fit.
claims.procedure: Evidence codes (F2.x) among confirmed F5.1 fragments, by conditions failed (exploratory E19).
claims.caveat: Post hoc refinements of the boundary account would be exploratory.

findings.previous_headline: The most common genuine failure was missing that a passage never reaches an evaluative judgment: models passed conclusions that discuss performance without ever saying how good it was. The study's calibration examples made this worse, even though the "not sound" example was itself a passage with no judgment.

findings.research_question: How do failure patterns vary across model families (frontier vs. open-source) and prompting conditions (zero-shot vs. few-shot)?
findings.headline: Choosing an open-source or closed model is unlikely to change accuracy, though it may change leniency: the two families matched on accuracy, but the open-source models called 6–8 points more passages sound, with and without examples.

claims.text: Families matched on accuracy: closed 60.9% vs open 58.9% (p = .39); six models indistinguishable (p = .66).
claims.procedure: H.2 two-proportion z-test (closed vs open) and chi-squared across six models (pre-specified).

claims.text: Open models called more passages sound and were more lenient than closed models, with and without examples; families did not differ in accuracy.
claims.procedure: Majority labels pooled by family and condition; closed - open contrasts with fragment-clustered bootstrap CIs (5,000, seed 42).
claims.caveat: Three models per family (purposive, top-performing); CIs resample passages, not models.

findings.research_question: How do failure patterns vary across model families (frontier vs. open-source) and prompting conditions (zero-shot vs. few-shot)?
findings.headline: Calibration examples can introduce bias that accuracy scores hide: a balanced, expert-written pair shifted five of six models toward calling reasoning sound, without reliably improving accuracy.

claims.text: 142 of 156 verdict changes between conditions (91%) went from not sound to sound; strong for four models (p < .0001), modest for GLM (p = .04), absent for Gemini.
claims.procedure: Paired by fragment within model: majority labels zero-shot vs few-shot; exact McNemar (binomial) test on the direction of discordant pairs.
claims.caveat: Does not use the gold standard. GLM's p would not survive a six-test correction.

claims.text: Accuracy barely moved because changes cut both ways: across all 156 changes, 90 fixed an error and 66 created one; pooled pass rate 58.6% to 61.2% (p = .067); only DeepSeek gained significantly.
claims.procedure: Each changed verdict scored against the locked gold; H.2 McNemar on paired fragment pass/fail.

claims.text: With examples, models converged at a more lenient level: spread in share called sound 44 to 34 points; model-model kappa 0.45 to 0.49; run-to-run unanimity 85.9% to 87.7%; 55-89% called sound vs the expert's 51%.
claims.procedure: Range of per-model share called sound by condition; mean pairwise Cohen's kappa between models; share of combinations with 3/3 run agreement.

findings.previous_headline: A balanced, expert-written pair of calibration examples shifted five of six models toward calling reasoning sound, without reliably improving accuracy.

findings.research_question: How do failure patterns vary across model families (frontier vs. open-source) and prompting conditions (zero-shot vs. few-shot)?
findings.headline: Calibration examples affected both families alike: they shifted closed and open models toward "sound" by similar amounts (13 vs 15 points) and improved accuracy in neither.

claims.text: Calibration examples shifted both families toward 'sound' by similar amounts (13 vs 15 points); the crossing on share called sound and on pass rate is not distinguishable from zero.
claims.procedure: Zero- to few-shot change within each family and the closed - open difference in change (difference in differences), bootstrap CIs.
claims.caveat: The leniency-ratio crossing excludes zero but ratios grow faster from a more lenient base; the linear measure shows no clear crossing.

RQ2.answer: Models were lenient judges of evaluative conclusions, especially on longer passages and with calibration examples, most often by passing conclusions that never reach a judgment.

RQ4.answer: Model families did not differ in accuracy, but the open-source models were somewhat more lenient. The calibration examples increased leniency in both families alike, without significantly improving accuracy.

RQ1.answer: LLMs agreed with the expert 60% of the time, barely better than a coin flip but about as often as trained human evaluators did, and they erred toward leniency.
